title: Atmospheric River Tracking Method Intercomparison Project (ARTMIP): project goals and experimental design
abstract: Abstract. The Atmospheric River Tracking Method Intercomparison Project (ARTMIP) is an international collaborative effort to understand and quantify the uncertainties in atmospheric river (AR) science based on detection algorithm alone. Currently, there are many AR identification and tracking algorithms in the literature with a wide range of techniques and conclusions. ARTMIP strives to provide the community with information on different methodologies and provide guidance on the most appropriate algorithm for a given science question or region of interest. All ARTMIP participants will implement their detection algorithms on a specified common dataset for a defined period of time. The project is divided into two phases: Tier 1 will utilize the Modern-Era Retrospective analysis for Research and Applications, version 2 (MERRA-2) reanalysis from January 1980 to June 2017 and will be used as a baseline for all subsequent comparisons. Participation in Tier 1 is required. Tier 2 will be optional and include sensitivity studies designed around specific science questions, such as reanalysis uncertainty and climate change. High-resolution reanalysis and/or model output will be used wherever possible. Proposed metrics include AR frequency, duration, intensity, and precipitation attributable to ARs. Here, we present the ARTMIP experimental design, timeline, project requirements, and a brief description of the variety of methodologies in the current literature. We also present results from our 1-month “proof-of-concept” trial run designed to illustrate the utility and feasibility of the ARTMIP project.
problem: The wide variety of atmospheric river detection and tracking algorithms produces significantly different results for AR climatologies and impacts, creating uncertainty and making it difficult to objectively compare findings across studies.
method: This paper proposes the Atmospheric River Tracking Method Intercomparison Project (ARTMIP), a framework where participants apply their detection algorithms to a common dataset to systematically compare methods and quantify uncertainties in atmospheric river climatology, hydrology, and extreme events.
task: The task is to quantify uncertainties in atmospheric river (AR) science arising from different detection algorithms by establishing the goals and experimental design for a systematic tracking method intercomparison project (ARTMIP).
innovation: This paper presents the goals and experimental design for the Atmospheric River Tracking Method Intercomparison Project (ARTMIP), a collaborative framework to understand and quantify uncertainties in atmospheric river science by systematically comparing various detection algorithms using a common dataset.

Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are often associated with extreme winter storms and heavy precipitation along the west coasts of midlatitude continents, including the western US, western Europe, and Chile (e.g., Ralph et al., 2004; Neiman et al., 2008; Viale and Nuñez, 2011; Lavers and Villarini, 2015; Waliser and Guan, 2107).

Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are often associated with extreme winter storms and heavy precipitation along the west coasts of midlatitude continents, including the western US, western Europe, and Chile (e.g., Ralph et al., 2004; Neiman et al., 2008; Viale and Nuñez, 2011; Lavers and Villarini, 2015; Waliser and Guan, 2107).

Despite their short-term hazards (e.g., landslides, flooding), ARs provide long-term benefits to regions such as California, where they contribute substantially to mountain snowpack (e.g., Guan et al., 2010), and ultimately refill reservoirs.

Their influence stretches as far as the polar caps as ARs transfer large amounts of heat and moisture poleward, influencing the ice sheets’ surface mass and energy budget (Gorodetskaya et al., 2014; Neff et al., 2014; Bonne et al., 2015).

For the full catalogues in Tier 1, additional regions will be analyzed, including the east Antarctic, which has proven to have large differences between methodologies that implement a global algorithm compared to a regionally specific polar algorithm (Gorodetskaya et al., 2014).

Many of the ARTMIP participants focus on the North Pacific (western North America) and North Atlantic (European) regions; however, ARs in other regions, such as the poles and the southeast US may also be evaluated with ARTMIP data.
